newsitem.title: Hungary: Hungary, Turkey sign free trade agreement.
newsitem.headline: Hungary, Turkey sign free trade agreement.

text.p: Turkey and Hungary signed a free trade agreement on Wednesday which both believe will smooth their path towards full European Union (EU) membership.

"This agreement marks an important step towards both countries' European economic integration," State Minister Ayfer Yilmaz told a joint press conference with Hungarian Industry and Trade Minister Szabolcs Fazakas after the signing ceremony.

The agreement, the first Turkey has signed with a country of central and eastern Europe, took almost four years to negotiate and removes tariffs on 90 percent of all industrial goods immediately, to be extended to 100 percent by 2001.
Current textile regulations will remain for one more year while agriculture, although exempted from total free trade, will be subject to new, easier quotas on goods worth up to $13 million.
Turkey's free trade agreement with the EU on coal and steel products will be extended to Hungary from January 1, 1999.
Both countries expect the agreement to boost bilateral trade to as much as $500 million a year from the current levels of below $200 million.
Yilmaz added that the deal was an important part of Turkish efforts to fulfil its pledges to a customs union agreement with the European Union (EU) which took effect last year.

Turkey entered into the lucrative customs deal with the EU from January 1996 which abolished customs duties in many industrial products and envisaged a common policy towards trade with third countries.

Yilmaz said the agreement with Hungary was the first step to creating a Europe-wide free trade zone incorporating the European Union, the former communist countries of central and eastern Europe and Turkey.
Free trade agreements, which include trade of industrial goods, some agricultural products and processed food items, bring Turkey in line with the EU terms in trade with third countries.

Yilmaz said a similar agreement with Israel, signed in March last year, and which was approved by the Israeli parliament, will eventually be passed by Turkey's parliament despite a delay since the current Turkish government was elected last year.
She denied the agreement was opposed by the Islamist wing of the Turkish cabinet, who are reported to have held up the deal because of their opposition to developing ties with Israel.
"These are complicated agreements," she said. "It is sometimes difficult to put them in place."
